t: An insurer issues a fire policy for sum insured ₹24 crore. Its facilities are: net retention ₹40 lakh, 1st surplus treaty of 15 lines, 2nd surplus treaty of 10 lines and a facultative obligatory treaty of ₹8 crore; the balance is placed facultatively. A claim of ₹1.2 crore is settled in full. The 1st surplus treaty's share of the claim is
e: All arrangements are proportional, so the claim is shared in the ratio of sums insured. 1st surplus capacity = 15 × ₹40 lakh = ₹6 crore, i.e. 6/24 of the risk; 6/24 × ₹1.2 crore = ₹30 lakh (retention ₹2 lakh, 2nd surplus ₹20 lakh, F/O ₹40 lakh, facultative ₹28 lakh).

t: In the same programme (sum insured ₹24 crore; retention ₹40 lakh; 1st surplus 15 lines; 2nd surplus 10 lines; facultative obligatory ₹8 crore), the amount that has to be placed by facultative reinsurance is
e: Automatic capacity = ₹0.40 + ₹6 + ₹4 + ₹8 crore = ₹18.4 crore. Balance ₹24 − ₹18.4 = ₹5.6 crore must be reinsured facultatively.

t: A risk excess of loss cover is ₹40 lakh in excess of ₹10 lakh, shared by reinsurer A 70% and reinsurer B 30%. A ground-up loss of ₹65 lakh occurs. The amount finally borne by the ceding insurer is
e: Loss above the priority is ₹55 lakh but the cover limit is ₹40 lakh, so reinsurers pay ₹40 lakh (A ₹28 lakh, B ₹12 lakh). The cedant bears the ₹10 lakh priority plus the ₹15 lakh above the layer = ₹25 lakh.

t: An insurer has a stop loss cover for 80% of all losses in excess of a 70% loss ratio. Premium income for the year is ₹60 crore and losses are ₹51 crore. The recovery from reinsurers is
e: 70% of ₹60 crore = ₹42 crore. Losses in excess = ₹51 − ₹42 = ₹9 crore. Reinsurers pay 80% of ₹9 crore = ₹7.2 crore; the balance 20% is co-retained by the cedant.

t: An insurer underwrites fire business on PML basis with: net retention ₹30 lakh PML; quota share 20% with limit ₹1.5 crore PML; 1st surplus 15 lines, limit ₹4.5 crore PML; 2nd surplus 20 lines, limit ₹6 crore PML. A risk of sum insured ₹40 crore is assessed at 30% PML. The cession to the 2nd surplus treaty is
e: Amount to be reinsured = 30% of ₹40 crore = ₹12 crore. Retention ₹0.30 crore; quota share 20% of ₹12 crore = ₹2.4 crore but limited to ₹1.5 crore; 1st surplus 15 × ₹30 lakh = ₹4.5 crore; balance ₹12 − 6.3 = ₹5.7 crore goes to the 2nd surplus (within its ₹6 crore limit), so nothing is placed facultatively.

t: GNPI for three years was ₹250 lakh, ₹300 lakh and ₹350 lakh, and losses incurred to the XL layer were ₹9 lakh, ₹12 lakh and ₹15 lakh respectively. With a loading factor of 100/80 the loaded burning cost is
e: Pure burning cost = total incurred losses ÷ total GNPI = 36/900 = 4%. Loaded burning cost = 4% × 100/80 = 5%.

t: An XL treaty is rated on burning cost with loading 100/70, subject to a minimum rate of 3% and maximum of 5%. GNPI is ₹8 crore and incurred claims to the cover were ₹12 lakh. The XL premium payable is
e: Burning cost = 12/800 = 1.5%; loaded = 1.5 × 100/70 = 2.14%, which is below the treaty minimum of 3%. Premium is therefore charged at 3% of ₹8 crore = ₹24 lakh.

topic: Excess of loss premium - maximum rate
t: GNPI ₹6 crore; incurred losses to the XL cover ₹54 lakh; rate 100/70 of burning cost, minimum 5%, maximum 10%. The XL premium chargeable is
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Burning cost = 54/600 = 9%; loaded = 9 × 100/70 = 12.86%, which exceeds the maximum. Premium is charged at the maximum 10% of ₹6 crore = ₹60 lakh.

t: An XL cover of ₹75 lakh xs ₹25 lakh carries a premium rate of 100/75 of burning cost, minimum 4% and maximum 8%, on GNPI of ₹4 crore. Deposit premium of ₹10 lakh was paid in two half-yearly instalments. Incurred losses to the cover were ₹30 lakh. The balance adjustment premium payable to reinsurers at year end is
e: Burning cost = 30/400 = 7.5%; loaded = 7.5 × 100/75 = 10%, which exceeds the maximum of 8%. Premium = 8% of ₹4 crore = ₹32 lakh; less deposit ₹10 lakh already paid = ₹22 lakh balance.

t: An XL cover of ₹60 lakh xs ₹15 lakh is rated at 3% of GNPI ₹2 crore. One reinstatement at 100% additional premium, pro rata to amount only, is provided. A loss results in a recovery of ₹24 lakh from reinsurers. The reinstatement premium is
e: XL premium = 3% × ₹2 crore = ₹6 lakh. Reinstatement premium = (loss recovery ÷ cover limit) × XL premium × 100% = 24/60 × ₹6 lakh = ₹2,40,000.

topic: Reinstatement premium - pro rata to time
t: Treaty period 1.4.2024 to 31.3.2025; cover ₹30 lakh xs ₹10 lakh; final XL premium ₹1,20,000; a ground-up loss of ₹25 lakh occurs on 6.11.2024; one reinstatement at 50% of annual premium, pro rata to amount and to time. The reinstatement premium is

An XL layer of ₹2 crore xs ₹50 lakh is rated at 5% on GNPI of ₹10 crore, with one reinstatement at 100% additional premium (pro rata to amount). The only loss of the year produced a recovery of ₹40 lakh. A reinsurer writing a 20% share of the layer has made a
e: XL premium = ₹50 lakh; reinstatement premium = 40/200 × ₹50 lakh = ₹10 lakh. 20% share: premium ₹10 lakh + reinstatement ₹2 lakh − loss ₹8 lakh = profit ₹4 lakh.

t: A buffer XL cover of ₹60 lakh xs ₹20 lakh also carries an aggregate annual deductible of 2% of GNPI. GNPI is ₹12.5 crore. Ground-up losses during the year were ₹32 lakh, ₹45 lakh and ₹38 lakh. Total recovery from reinsurers is
e: Aggregate deductible = 2% of ₹12.5 crore = ₹25 lakh. Excess over ₹20 lakh: 12 + 25 + 18 = ₹55 lakh. The first ₹25 lakh of excess is absorbed by the aggregate deductible (12 from loss 1 and 13 from loss 2); reinsurers pay 12 on loss 2 and 18 on loss 3 = ₹30 lakh.

topic: Catastrophe excess of loss - hours clause
t: A cat XL cover of ₹30 lakh xs ₹10 lakh per loss occurrence has a 72-hours clause. Floods lasting 8 days produce losses of ₹35 lakh in the first 72 hours, ₹50 lakh in the next 72 hours and ₹12 lakh in the final 48 hours. The total recovery is
e: Each 72-hour period is one occurrence: period I ₹35 − 10 = ₹25 lakh; period II ₹50 − 10 = 40, limited to ₹30 lakh; period III ₹12 − 10 = ₹2 lakh. Total ₹57 lakh.

t: Treaty account data (100%): premium ₹5,00,000; commission 40%; taxes and charges ₹12,000; claims paid ₹2,40,000 (including a cash loss of ₹25,000 already paid by reinsurers); premium reserve retained 40%; previous year's premium reserve released ₹1,80,000; XL premium for common account ₹4,000. The balance due to reinsurers for a reinsurer with a 15% share is
e: Credits: premium 5,00,000 + reserve released 1,80,000 + cash loss credit 25,000 = 7,05,000. Debits: commission 2,00,000 + taxes 12,000 + claims 2,40,000 + reserve retained 2,00,000 + XL premium 4,000 = 6,56,000. Balance ₹49,000 due to reinsurers; 15% = ₹7,350.

t: First surplus treaty, year 2024-25: premium ₹60 lakh; commission 35%; claims paid ₹18 lakh; management expenses 5% of premium; portfolio entry: premium 40% of previous year's premium of ₹50 lakh and losses 100% of previous year's outstanding of ₹8 lakh; portfolio withdrawal: premium 40% of current premium and losses 100% of current outstanding of ₹11 lakh. Profit commission at 20% amounts to
e: Income = 60 + 20 + 8 = ₹88 lakh. Outgo = commission 21 + claims 18 + ME 3 + premium withdrawal 24 + loss withdrawal 11 = ₹77 lakh. Profit ₹11 lakh × 20% = ₹2.2 lakh.

t: A treaty provides profit commission of 25% on profit up to 10% of ceded premium and 60% on the balance profit. Premium ceded is ₹60 lakh and net adjusted profit is ₹9 lakh. Total profit commission is
e: 10% of premium = ₹6 lakh: 25% = ₹1.5 lakh. Balance profit ₹3 lakh: 60% = ₹1.8 lakh. Total super profit commission = ₹3.3 lakh.

t: Profit commission is payable at 20% on the three-year average system. Treaty results were: 2022-23 profit ₹9 lakh, 2023-24 loss ₹3 lakh, 2024-25 profit ₹12 lakh. Profit commission for 2024-25 is
e: Average = (9 − 3 + 12)/3 = ₹6 lakh; 20% of ₹6 lakh = ₹1.2 lakh. The loss year is averaged in, reducing the commission.

t: Premiums ceded to a treaty during the year were ₹2,50,000; the premium reserve brought forward was ₹90,000 and the reserve carried forward is ₹1,00,000. Earned premium is
e: Earned premium = premiums ceded + reserve brought forward − reserve carried forward = 2,50,000 + 90,000 − 1,00,000 = ₹2,40,000.

t: GNPI for four years: ₹200, ₹220, ₹260 and ₹320 lakh; losses to the XL layer: ₹10, ₹15, ₹8 and ₹17 lakh. The pure burning cost is
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Pure burning cost = total losses ÷ total GNPI = 50/1000 = 5%. A loading of 100/70 would give a loaded rate of 7.14%.

t: Under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, a reinsurance document chargeable with duty that has been executed outside India
o: need not be stamped at all
must be stamped before it is signed abroad
must be stamped within 30 days of execution abroad
must be stamped within 3 months of its receipt in India
e: Documents executed out of India may be stamped within three months after they are first received in India. Documents executed in India must be stamped at or before execution.

t: For marine cargo reinsurance the arrangement frequently used is
o: a combination of quota share and surplus treaty
e: Cargo portfolios have many small-to-medium risks, so a quota share plus surplus combination is common; hull business more commonly uses surplus treaties.

t: The three types of retention referred to in the material are per risk, per event and
e: Retention may be fixed per risk, per event (accumulation from one occurrence) and per portfolio (aggregate for a class in a year, protected by stop loss).

t: The statement that 'most present-day treaties are blind' means that
o: the reinsurer does not know the identity of the cedant
the ceding company supplies no details of individual cessions to the reinsurer
the treaty has no stated limit
reinsurers accept the treaty without a slip
e: Blind treaties are administered on a bordereau-free basis; the reinsurer receives only periodical accounts, not particulars of each risk ceded.

t: The 'follow the fortunes' clause means that the reinsurer
o: takes over the financial fortunes of the ceding insurer, including its investment losses
pays claims regardless of the terms and conditions of the reinsurance contract
shares the insurance fortunes of the cedant as expressed in the reinsurance contract
is bound by ex gratia payments of any amount
e: The reinsurer follows the underwriting (insurance) fortunes of the cedant on risks ceded, within the terms of the treaty; it does not follow its general commercial fortunes.

t: In treaty wordings NCAD stands for
o: Notice of continuation at anniversary date
Notice of cancellation at anniversary date
e: NCAD (notice of cancellation at anniversary date) is the standard mechanism under the commencement and termination clause, usually requiring a stated period of notice such as three months.

t: In the cover above (final premium ₹72 lakh) a deposit premium of ₹40 lakh was paid during the year. At adjustment the cedant
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Adjusted premium ₹72 lakh less deposit ₹40 lakh = ₹32 lakh payable to reinsurers.

t: Under a typical hours clause, the duration of any one loss occurrence for a catastrophe other than windstorm, earthquake or riot is commonly
e: The usual hours clause provides 72 hours for hurricane/typhoon/windstorm/hail, 72 hours for earthquake and related perils, 72 hours within one city/town for riot and civil commotion, and 168 hours for any other catastrophe.

t: A cut-through clause gives the original insured
o: the right to inspect the reinsurer's books
the right to cancel the reinsurance
e: A cut-through clause provides that, in the event of the reinsured's insolvency, the reinsurer's share of a loss may be paid directly to the original insured.

t: The entire amount of an insured loss including the deductible but before salvage and recoveries is called
e: Ground-up loss is the total loss from the first rupee; ultimate net loss is the amount after deductions and recoveries that is tested against the XL priority.

t: No reinsurance commission is normally payable to the ceding company under
e: Under non-proportional covers the reinsurer charges a price for the layer (a rate on GNPI); the cedant's acquisition costs are not reimbursed by commission.

t: The difference between estimated maximum loss (EML) and probable maximum loss (PML) is that EML is assessed within the realms of
e: EML is the maximum loss that could affect a single risk within the realms of possibility; PML is within the realms of probability. Both disregard unlikely coincidences and catastrophes and are used for material damage only.

t: As a rule the leading reinsurer on a treaty
o: has the largest share and sets the terms
takes no share but only sets terms
e: The lead reinsurer negotiates the terms (for example the XL rate), signs the slip first and usually carries the largest line; others follow its terms.

t: Non-disclosure of a material fact by the proposer makes the contract:
o: Voidable at the option of the insurer
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Breach of utmost good faith renders the contract voidable, not void; the insurer may elect to avoid it (subject to Section 45 for life).

t: Before 2006-07 the obligatory cession by Indian non-life insurers to the Indian reinsurer was
e: The statutory cession was 20% up to 2006-07, reduced to 15% in 2007-08, 10% from 2008-09, 5% from 2013-14 and 4% from 2022-23 onwards.

t: Under a typical arbitration clause in a reinsurance agreement, disputes are resolved by
o: each party appointing an arbiter, the two appointing an umpire, with a majority decision binding
a court of competent jurisdiction only
the leading reinsurer acting as sole arbiter
e: The arbitration clause provides a means of resolving differences without litigation: each side appoints an arbiter, the two choose a third (umpire) and the majority decision binds both parties.

t: A newly licensed general insurer with limited capital and no claims experience of its own wants to build a fire portfolio. The treaty form most suitable at this stage is
e: Quota share is preferred by a newly formed company with limited experience and capital: it gives the reinsurer a balanced share of every risk, is simple to administer and earns a higher ceding commission.

t: An insurer writing crop insurance against pest damage over widely dispersed areas wants protection against an unusually high loss ratio in a bad year. The suitable arrangement is
e: Stop loss protects the annual result of a class against an unusually high frequency of small losses, which is the exposure in widely dispersed agricultural business.

t: Under a working XL treaty of ₹20 lakh xs ₹5 lakh, the claims department settles a loss of ₹4.5 lakh. The reinsurers' liability on this loss is
o: nil, as the loss is within the priority
e: Claims falling below the priority (retention) are paid fully by the reinsured; the XL reinsurer responds only when the ultimate net loss exceeds the priority.

t: A liability XL treaty contains an index (stability) clause. During a period of high inflation the effect of this clause is to
o: increase the XL premium rate automatically
adjust the priority and the cover limit so that their relative monetary values are maintained
cancel the treaty if inflation exceeds a stated rate
e: The stability clause provides a formula for recalculating the priority and the reinsurer's liability so that inflation does not shift an increasing share of long-tail losses onto the reinsurer.

t: A large fire claim of ₹3 crore has just been settled and the ceding insurer needs funds immediately rather than waiting for the quarterly treaty account. It should invoke the
e: The cash loss clause allows the cedant to call for immediate payment of the reinsurers' share of a loss exceeding the agreed cash loss limit; the amount is then credited in the next account.

t: A reinsurer owes the cedant ₹18 lakh towards claims while the cedant owes the reinsurer ₹25 lakh of premium. Under the set-off clause the settlement is
o: the cedant pays the net ₹7 lakh
each party pays the full amount it owes
the reinsurer pays ₹18 lakh and the premium is deferred
no payment until the year-end account
e: The set-off (offset) clause permits each party to net amounts due against those payable before settlement; it is especially valuable if one party becomes insolvent.

t: A cedant's fire treaty is on a 'worldwide' basis. Owing to differing laws and insurance practice, the countries usually excluded from such a treaty are
o: the United States of America and Canada
e: Worldwide treaties customarily exclude the USA and Canada because of their litigation environment and divergent insurance practice; such risks need special acceptance.

topic: Excess of loss - liability of reinsurer
t: A claim of ₹90 lakh on a risk protected by an XL cover of ₹50 lakh xs ₹20 lakh is still under investigation and has not been admitted by the insurer. The XL reinsurer's liability
o: arises immediately on intimation of the claim
arises only when the loss is admitted by the insurer and the ultimate net loss exceeds the retention
is to pay ₹90 lakh and recover from the cedant
e: Under XL the reinsurer is liable only after the cedant has admitted the loss and the UNL exceeds the priority; it then pays the excess up to the limit, the balance above the limit reverting to the cedant.

t: A cold storage was reinsured facultatively for the policy year ending 31 March. The branch renews the policy on 1 April without further reference to the reinsurance department. The facultative reinsurer
o: is not on risk, because facultative cover starts and expires with the original policy
is automatically on risk for the renewed policy
is on risk for 30 days of grace
is on risk only if a renewal bordereau is sent
e: Facultative cover is for a single policy and period; it starts and expires with the original policy, so renewal requires a fresh facultative placement.

t: Before placing a treaty, the reinsurance department carries out 'security vetting'. This means
o: checking the physical security of the cedant's offices
verifying that the slip is stamped
obtaining a bank guarantee from the broker
an analysis of the financial standing of the proposed reinsurer
e: Security vetting is the assessment of a reinsurer's financial strength and rating so that the cedant is not exposed to an uncollectible recovery.

t: Deduction for life insurance premium under Section 80C of the Income Tax Act is available up to an overall limit of:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). ₹1,50,000 aggregate for all 80C items; premium qualifies only up to 10% of the sum assured for policies issued after 1 April 2012.

t: A broker issues a cover note after completing a facultative placement. Legally the cover note is
o: a non-binding memorandum pending the treaty wording
a preliminary but binding document stating the main terms agreed, pending the formal wording
e: The cover note evidences the placement and is binding on the reinsurers who have subscribed, even though the full wording follows later.

t: A reinsurer retires from a quota share treaty at 31 December and a new reinsurer takes its share. Under the clean-cut method
o: premium and loss portfolios are withdrawn from the outgoing reinsurer at year end and credited as entries to the incoming reinsurer
the outgoing reinsurer continues to pay losses on policies it had accepted until they expire
the cedant retains all unexpired liability
the incoming reinsurer pays no portfolio premium
e: Clean-cut (portfolio transfer) terminates the outgoing reinsurer's liability by withdrawing premium and loss portfolios, which are simultaneously entered to the renewing reinsurers.

t: A premium reserve deposit retained by the ceding company under a proportional treaty
o: belongs to the cedant and is never released
is held as security for the reinsurer's share of unearned premium and released with interest in the following year
is paid over to the broker
is a fine for late accounts
e: The cedant withholds an agreed percentage of premium (and sometimes of outstanding losses) as a guarantee of the reinsurer's performance, usually paying interest on it and releasing it in the next year's account.
